papers.title: Convergence and error analysis of problem-independent machine learning (PIML) with linear completeness
papers.label: arXiv:2611.32293v1

summary.one_liner: The paper gives an error analysis for problem-independent machine learning (PIML), which uses neural networks to predict finite element shape functions, and proposes a linearly complete variant whose H1 and L2 convergence is established.
summary.plain: Engineers often simulate how structures bend or stretch by splitting them into small pieces and computing how each piece responds. A method called PIML speeds this up by training a neural network to produce these piece-by-piece response rules, so they do not have to be recalculated each time. This paper checks how accurate that approach is in theory, and finds that a simple version can fail to improve as the mesh gets finer, so the authors add a fix.
summary.why: Faster simulation of repeated structural pieces matters for design and analysis work. The paper's main value is in showing that a basic learned version carries an error that does not shrink under mesh refinement, and that adding linear-field constraints restores convergence with optimal rates in the tested cases. Its broader relevance to other machine-learning-plus-simulation methods is plausible but not shown in the text.
summary.background:
- Finite element method (FEM): approximating a physical field by splitting a domain into small elements (a mesh) and solving on it.
- Mesh refinement: making the elements smaller; a good method's error should shrink as this happens.
- Substructuring: solving a large structure by treating repeated or reusable pieces separately.
- Shape functions: the rules that describe how displacement varies inside an element.
- Rigid-body displacement invariance: a rigid shift or rotation of a piece should produce no internal stress.
- Linear completeness: the method must reproduce simple linear displacement fields exactly; this is a standard requirement for convergence.
- H1 and L2 norms: ways of measuring error in the function and its gradient (H1) or the function alone (L2).
- Generalization error: how far a trained network's predictions are from correct values on inputs it was not trained on.

papers.abstract: Problem-independent machine learning (PIML) is an effective computational approach that combines the finite element method with machine learning. PIML uses neural networks to learn the mapping from material distributions or element geometries to the numerical shape functions of substructures. This approach avoids repeated computation while preserving the conformity of the underlying finite element discretization, thereby significantly improving the efficiency of substructure-based finite element analysis. However, existing studies on PIML have primarily focused on numerical accuracy and computational efficiency, while rigorous theoretical analyses of its approximation errors are still limited. In this paper, we establish an error analysis framework for PIML from a classical finite element perspective, in which the numerical error is bounded in terms of the finite element discretization error and the network generalization error. Our analysis shows that, when only rigid-body displacement invariance is enforced, the resulting error estimate contains a learning-induced term that does not necessarily decrease under mesh refinement. To ensure convergence, we propose an improved PIML scheme with linear completeness. By using linear displacement field constraints to reconstruct the corresponding columns of the transition matrix, we ensure that the resulting numerical shape-function space contains the space of linear polynomials. We derive error estimates and establish convergence results of the improved scheme in the H1 and L2 norms. Numerical experiments verify the theoretical results and demonstrate that the improved PIML achieves optimal convergence rates, good generalization performance, and numerical stability.

papers.title: Uncertainty Quantification and Global Sensitivity Analysis of Patient-Specific Coronary Hemodynamics Under Unsteady Flow Conditions
papers.label: arXiv:2611.31594v1

summary.one_liner: This paper applies polynomial chaos expansion-based uncertainty quantification and global sensitivity analysis to finite element simulations of patient-specific coronary hemodynamics under pulsatile flow, quantifying how input uncertainty propagates to wall shear stress, oscillatory shear index, and cross-flow index across three patients.
summary.plain: Computer models of blood flow in a patient's heart arteries can guide diagnosis and treatment, but their inputs (blood pressure, viscosity, density, heart rate, and flow shape) are never known exactly. This study treats those inputs as uncertain, runs many simulations efficiently using a statistical emulator, and measures how much each input drives the spread in key flow-related measures on the artery wall. The authors report that steady wall-friction averages were mainly shaped by flow speed and blood viscosity, while measures of back-and-forth or multidirectional wall forces were dominated by the uncertainty in the flow waveform.
summary.why: Clinical use of such models depends on knowing how much their predictions can be trusted, so quantifying input uncertainty bears directly on confidence in simulated markers of disease. The text does not show clinical validation or outcomes, so its practical impact remains unclear from this abstract alone.
summary.background:
- Coronary arteries supply blood to the heart muscle; patient-specific models are built from a person's imaging data.
- Wall shear stress (WSS) is the frictional force blood exerts on the artery lining; it is linked in the literature to disease development.
- Oscillatory shear index and cross-flow index are summary measures of how wall forces change direction over a heartbeat.
- Finite element method: a standard numerical technique for solving fluid equations on a mesh.
- Uncertainty quantification: estimating how uncertain inputs spread into uncertain outputs.
- Polynomial chaos expansion: a fast surrogate that approximates the model with polynomials, so many runs can be replaced by cheap evaluations.
- Global sensitivity analysis: splitting output variance into shares due to each input and their interactions.
- Coefficient of variation: spread divided by mean, a unitless measure of relative variability.
- Principal component analysis: a way to summarize the main shape variations in a set of waveforms.

papers.abstract: Patient-specific computational models of the coronary arteries demonstrate transformative potential for physiological assessment, identifying hemodynamic markers associated with disease progression, and optimizing treatment. Unfortunately, these models rarely account for input parameter uncertainty, limiting confidence in predictions and their clinical interpretation. Herein, we present a novel uncertainty quantification-finite element framework that integrates computationally efficient techniques to characterize and propagate uncertainty through patient-specific coronary simulations under unsteady flow conditions. Principal component analysis characterized variability in pulsatile coronary velocity waveforms, while uncertainty in blood pressure, viscosity, density, and heart rate is represented through probability distributions. Polynomial chaos expansion (PCE) enabled efficient uncertainty propagation and global sensitivity analysis across three patient-specific models, quantifying variability in time-averaged wall shear stress (WSS), oscillatory shear index, and cross-flow index. Fourth-order PCE emulators converged across all three patients, yielding analyses of 505 models per patient, with median coefficients of variation ranging from 0.15-0.20 for time-averaged WSS, 0.54-0.75 for oscillatory shear index, and 0.28-0.38 for cross-flow index, highlighting greater relative uncertainty in multidirectional WSS metrics. Global sensitivity analysis revealed that time-averaged WSS variability was governed by the individual effects of velocity and blood viscosity, with parameter interactions contributing <2% of total variance. In contrast, velocity waveform uncertainty dominated variability in the oscillatory shear index and cross-flow index, with higher-order parameter interactions accounting for 20.7-34.5% and 26.6-37.8% of total variance, respectively.

papers.title: An adaptive finite element method for the interior problem of Helmholtz equations with generalized transmission boundary conditions
papers.label: arXiv:2611.32479v1

summary.background:
- Helmholtz equation: a standard equation describing steady wave behavior (sound, light, water waves) at a fixed frequency.
- Interior transmission problem: a setup where waves are coupled across the boundary of a region, with conditions on both sides of that boundary.
- Generalized transmission boundary conditions: rules that specify how the wave and its normal derivative must match across an interface, here including a surface term.
- Laplace-Beltrami operator: a differential operator describing how a quantity varies along a curved surface, analogous to a Laplacian restricted to the surface.
- Finite element method: a numerical technique that splits a domain into small pieces (a mesh) and solves for an approximate solution on them.
- Adaptive / a posteriori error estimates: methods that compute the error from the approximate solution itself and refine the mesh where the error is largest.
- T-coercivity and lifting operators: advanced functional-analysis tools used to prove that the variational problem has a unique, stable solution.
- Interior transmission eigenvalues: special frequencies at which the interior transmission problem has nontrivial solutions.
summary.one_liner: The paper develops and analyzes an adaptive finite element method, with a-priori and a-posteriori error estimates, for the interior transmission problem of Helmholtz equations with generalized transmission boundary conditions involving a surface Laplace-Beltrami operator, using T-coercivity and a lifting operator to establish well-posedness in nonstandard Sobolev spaces.
summary.plain: This paper is about a method for computing wave behavior at the boundary between two materials, where waves can pass through the interface and the interface itself has its own surface behavior. The authors build a computer method that refines its mesh where errors are largest, prove it is mathematically sound, and test it on numerical examples. They also apply the method to find special resonant frequencies (interior transmission eigenvalues) of the problem.
summary.why: Computing accurate wave solutions with complicated interface conditions matters for modeling scattering and inverse problems in acoustics and electromagnetics. The text reports numerical examples showing accuracy and convergence, but it does not say how the method compares with existing approaches beyond stating that it is efficient.

papers.abstract: This paper proposes a new adaptive finite element method for solving the interior transmission problem with generalized transmission boundary conditions (GTBCs) involving a surface Laplace-Beltrami operator. A $\mathbb{T}$-coercivity technique relying on a lifting operator is established to show the well-posedness of the variational problem in appropriate nonstandard Sobolev spaces. Then both the a priori error estimates and a posteriori error estimates including the upper bound and local lower bound of the finite element discretization are constructed. Numerical examples are presented to illustrate the accuracy and convergence of the adaptive finite element method. Extension and high efficiency of the proposed method for the computation of the interior transmission eigenvalues for the problem with GTBCs are also discussed numerically.

papers.title: Upwind finite element approximation of the gradient blow-up time for a viscous Hamilton--Jacobi equation
papers.label: arXiv:2611.31859v1

summary.background:
- Hamilton–Jacobi equation: a partial differential equation describing how a function evolves, often used for optimal control and front motion.
- Viscous term: a diffusion (smoothing) term that keeps solutions from becoming discontinuous too early.
- Gradient blow-up: the slope of the solution grows without bound in finite time, even though the solution itself stays bounded.
- Superquadratic source: a nonlinear growth term in the slope that grows faster than the square of the slope.
- Dirichlet boundary condition: the solution is fixed (here zero) on the edge of the domain.
- Finite element method: approximating a function by simple pieces (e.g., piecewise linear) on a mesh of small cells.
- Upwind scheme: a discretization that takes information from the direction the flow comes from, for stability.
- Maximum-norm convergence: the worst-case pointwise error goes to zero as the mesh is refined.
- Polytopal domain: a domain with straight-edged (polygonal/polyhedral) boundary approximating a smooth one.
summary.one_liner: The paper proves maximum-norm convergence of an upwind piecewise-linear finite element scheme, and convergence of computed gradient-blow-up times, for a viscous Hamilton–Jacobi equation with superquadratic gradient source on polytopal approximations of smooth domains in 1–3 dimensions, verified on the disk.
summary.plain: The paper studies a equation describing a quantity whose slope becomes infinitely steep in finite time, a "gradient blow-up." The authors use a computer method that splits the domain into small triangles or segments and uses a directional ("upwind") rule to handle the steep gradients. They prove that the computed solution approaches the true one before the steepening happens, and that the computed time of steepening approaches the true time, under stated conditions, with a worked example on a disk and numerical experiments.
summary.why: Getting the timing of a singularity right is hard for numerical methods, since small errors in a steep slope can shift the predicted event. The work gives rigorous error guarantees for this kind of problem rather than only plots, though the text does not say how it compares with other schemes or applications.

papers.abstract: We analyze an upwind finite element method with piecewise linear elements for a viscous Hamilton--Jacobi equation with a superquadratic gradient source term, subject to homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions. On polytopal inner approximations of smooth bounded domains in dimensions $N=1,2,3$, we prove maximum-norm convergence of the numerical solution to the exact solution before gradient blow-up and convergence of gradient-threshold times to the blow-up time under explicit mesh and regularity assumptions. We also verify the regularity assumption and finite-time gradient blow-up for an example on the disk, to which the main theorem therefore applies. Numerical experiments illustrate this gradient blow-up.

papers.title: On mesh transfers and time error estimation in adaptive finite element methods for parabolic problems
papers.label: arXiv:2611.29379v1

summary.background:
- Finite element method: a standard way to approximate solutions of partial differential equations by splitting space into a mesh of small cells.
- Parabolic problem / heat equation: a model of how a quantity such as temperature spreads over space and time.
- Implicit Euler method: a basic time-stepping scheme that advances the solution in small time steps.
- Adaptive mesh refinement: automatically making the mesh finer where the error is large, and coarser elsewhere, which requires transferring the solution between meshes.
- A posteriori error estimator: a computable quantity that estimates the size of the numerical error during the calculation, used to guide adaptivity.
- Elliptic reconstruction: an auxiliary smooth approximation of the discrete solution, used here as the basis of the new transfer.
- Residual: the amount by which an approximate solution fails to satisfy the governing equation.
summary.one_liner: The paper shows that transferring the discrete solution and its time derivative to a new spatial mesh in space-time adaptive finite element solvers for the heat equation (implicit Euler) can break the discrete equation, causing the time error estimator to overestimate local error by a factor inversely proportional to the time step, and proposes elliptic-reconstruction-based transfers to reduce or remove this residual.
summary.plain: Computer simulations of heat spreading often change the grid of points they use as they go, and each change requires copying the current solution onto the new grid. The paper points out that this copying, even when the grid is only refined, can leave a mismatch that makes the software's own error check too pessimistic for small time steps. The authors propose a different copying method, based on an elliptic reconstruction, that greatly reduces or removes this mismatch, and they test it on an adaptive example.
summary.why: Adaptive solvers rely on error estimates to decide where to refine and how large each time step can be, so a systematic overestimate can make them waste effort. The text only covers the implicit Euler method applied to the heat equation and a single adaptive example, so how far the findings extend to other methods or problems is not established here.

papers.abstract: In space and time adaptive finite element methods, the discrete solution is transferred onto a different mesh whenever the spatial mesh changes. Refinement is commonly regarded as harmless, since nodal interpolation then reproduces the discrete solution exactly. However, we show that for the implicit Euler method applied to the heat equation, the transferred solution and time derivative, in general, violate the discrete equation on the new mesh. Unless the resulting transfer residual vanishes, the corresponding time error estimator overestimates the local error, for small time steps, by a factor inversely proportional to the time step size. To address this issue, we propose transfers based on the elliptic reconstruction, which significantly reduce the transfer residual or even remove it. In numerical experiments, we confirm the analysis and demonstrate the advantages of the proposed transfers in a space and time adaptive example.

papers.title: A High-Order Geometry-Conforming Selective Discontinuous Galerkin Method and Its Error Analysis for Elliptic Interface Problems on Curved Domains
papers.label: arXiv:2611.30169v1

summary.one_liner: A high-order immersed finite element method on curved domains with interfaces, using a boundary-conforming triangular mesh, Frenet–Serret coordinates, and a symmetric selective discontinuous Galerkin formulation, with a priori error analysis giving O(h^m) energy and O(h^(m+1)) L2 bounds.
summary.plain:
The paper studies how to compute approximate solutions to physics-style equations (elliptic partial differential equations) where the material has an internal boundary, called an interface, inside a curved region. The mesh only has to match the outer curved edge, not the internal interface, which avoids costly remeshing. The authors build a high-order version of this method, prove how accurate it is, and report numerical tests that match the predicted convergence rates and show fewer unknowns than a fully discontinuous method.</plain>
<parameter name="why">Interface problems on curved domains appear in many engineering and science models, and a method that avoids meshing around interfaces while keeping accuracy and reducing unknowns may be useful there. The text itself only supports these modest claims about accuracy and degrees of freedom; its practical impact beyond the reported tests is not established here.</plain>
<parameter name="background">- Partial differential equation (PDE): an equation describing how a quantity such as heat or stress varies over space.
- Interface problem: a PDE where material properties jump across an internal boundary.
- Finite element method: approximating a solution with simple piecewise polynomial pieces on a mesh of small triangles.
- Mesh and degrees of freedom: the mesh is the set of small cells; degrees of freedom are the unknown values the computer solves for.
- Immersed finite element: a method whose elements need not align with the interface, so the interface can cut through them.
- Discontinuous Galerkin: a method that allows the approximate solution to jump between cells, weakly enforced through penalty terms.
- Error bound O(h^m): the error shrinks roughly like the mesh size h raised to power m; higher m means faster convergence.
- Energy norm and L2 norm: two ways of measuring the size of the error.
- Frenet–Serret coordinates: a local coordinate system that follows a curve, used to describe curved boundaries.
- Trace inequality: a bound relating a function's size on an element's boundary to its size inside.</background>
<parameter name="difficulty">research-level

papers.abstract: We develop and analyze a high-order geometry-conforming immersed finite element (GC-IFE) method for elliptic interface problems on curved domains. The method uses a triangular mesh that conforms to the outer boundary but need not fit the internal interface. Using Frenet--Serret coordinates, the method combines GC-IFE spaces on interface elements, geometry-conforming finite element spaces on curved boundary elements, and standard Lagrange spaces elsewhere. The global degrees of freedom of the proposed method are asymptotically the same as that of the standard continuous finite element method on the same mesh. The main analytical contributions are approximation estimates and trace inequalities for triangular GC-IFE functions. These estimates are used to establish stability and an optimal $O(h^m)$ error bound in an energy norm for the proposed method, which is based on a symmetric selective discontinuous Galerkin formulation. An optimal $O(h^{m+1})$ error bound in the $L^2$ norm is also obtained under the standard regularity assumption on the dual problem. Numerical experiments confirm theoretical convergence rates and demonstrate a reduction in global degrees of freedom to a fully discontinuous Galerkin method.

papers.title: Convergence of a finite element Chorin projection method for the stochastic Navier--Stokes equations
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27969v1

summary.background:
- Navier--Stokes equations: the standard equations describing how viscous fluids move.
- Incompressible: the fluid's density stays constant, so its velocity must be divergence free (no net sources or sinks).
- Stochastic / multiplicative noise: random forcing whose strength depends on the current state of the flow.
- Finite element method: splitting a domain into small pieces and approximating the solution with simple functions on them.
- Chorin projection method: a two-step time-stepping trick that first moves the flow forward, then corrects it to restore incompressibility.
- Martingale solution: a weak notion of a random solution, defined on a possibly different probability space, which need not be unique.
- Moment estimates and tightness: bounds on average sizes of the random quantities and a way to guarantee that a sequence of random paths has convergent subsequences.
- Aldous' criterion: a standard test for tightness of random processes.
- Vortex sheet: an idealized flow with a concentrated jump in velocity across a curve, a hard test case.
summary.one_liner: Proves that a fully discrete finite element Chorin projection scheme for the stochastic incompressible Navier--Stokes equations with multiplicative noise and Dirichlet boundary conditions converges (along a subsequence) to a martingale solution in two and three dimensions, under a coupling of space and time step sizes.
summary.plain: This paper studies a computer method for simulating fluid flow (like water or air) that is randomly disturbed by noise, where the fluid is kept incompressible and sits inside a container with fixed walls. The authors show that their step-by-step numerical scheme stays well-behaved and, as the grid gets finer, its results settle toward a valid random-solution of the underlying equations. They also test the method numerically in two dimensions on smooth and vortex-sheet starting conditions.
summary.why: Random fluid models are used when uncertainty or noise matters, so a convergence proof gives some confidence that the computed results mean something. The text does not say how the method compares with other schemes or what applications it targets, so its wider impact is uncertain.

papers.abstract: We analyze a fully discrete finite element projection method for the stochastic incompressible Navier--Stokes equations with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions and multiplicative noise. We show solvability and uniform moment estimates for the intermediate and the corrected velocity approximations under the assumption that the initial data is square-integrable and divergence free, and that the deterministic forcing term is bounded in $L^{q}(0,T;H^{-1}(D))$ for a sufficiently large $q$. Under standard stability and approximation assumptions on the finite element spaces and a coupling condition on the spatial and temporal discretization parameters, we prove convergence of a subsequence to a martingale solution of the stochastic Navier--Stokes equations. The analysis combines the complementary spatial and temporal estimates of the predicted and the corrected velocity approximations and uses the numerical dissipation to identify their common limit. We establish tightness of the piecewise constant temporal interpolations of the velocity field approximations using Aldous' criterion combined with the uniform discrete moment estimates. The convergence result holds in two and three space dimensions as it does not rely on any additional regularity of the limiting martingale solution beyond the one naturally available from the energy inequality. Finally, we demonstrate the performance of the scheme in numerical experiments in two space dimensions for smooth and vortex sheet initial data.

papers.title: A Validation-Driven Bilevel Optimization Method for Mesh-Free PDE Solvers and Its Error Analysis
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27347v1

summary.background:
- PDE (partial differential equation): an equation relating a function to its rates of change, used to model physical processes such as heat or waves.
- Mesh-free solver: a numerical method that works from scattered points rather than a fixed grid of cells.
- Residual: how far a candidate solution misses satisfying the equation at chosen points.
- Bilevel optimization: an outer problem (choose settings) wrapped around an inner problem (fit the solution to the settings).
- Validation set: held-out points used to score choices without fitting to them.
- Hypergradient: the gradient of the outer score with respect to the settings, which lets the outer choice be improved by gradient steps.
- Gauss-Newton method: an iterative method for nonlinear least-squares fitting; "damped" means step sizes are tempered for stability.
- Adjoint system: an auxiliary linear system used to compute hypergradients efficiently.
- Preconditioning: transforming a linear system so an iterative solver converges faster.
- Physics-informed neural network (PINN): a neural network trained to satisfy a PDE and its boundary conditions.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes a validation-driven bilevel optimization framework for tuning design parameters of mesh-free PDE solvers (Kansa, random feature/extreme learning machine, and physics-informed neural network methods), using an efficient implicit hypergradient with warm-started damped Gauss-Newton and preconditioned minimum-residual adjoint solves, and derives local error bounds linking validation residuals to solution accuracy.
summary.plain: Mesh-free methods solve equations like heat or fluid flow by checking the equation at scattered sample points instead of on a grid. These methods have settings, such as network shape or regularization strength, that strongly affect accuracy and are hard to choose. The authors choose these settings by fitting the solution on training points and scoring it on separate held-out validation points, and they make the search for good settings computationally cheaper for nonlinear equations.
summary.why: Choosing solver settings is a practical bottleneck for these methods, and a single selection framework that works across several solver families could be useful. The text reports numerical experiments, including a high-dimensional nonlinear problem, but I cannot judge from the abstract alone how large the practical gains are.

papers.abstract: Mesh-free partial differential equation (PDE) solvers construct discrete systems from residuals at sampled points. These solvers fit coefficients in a parameterized trial representation and select solver-design parameters governing the representation, training-residual weighting, and regularization. These parameters strongly affect solution accuracy, yet existing selection strategies are largely tailored to particular solver classes. To address this limitation, we formulate a unified validation-driven bilevel optimization framework applicable across different solver classes, in which the lower level fits coefficients using training collocation residuals, while the upper level selects solver-design parameters using held-out validation residuals. For nonlinear PDEs, however, solving the nonlinear lower-level problem to high accuracy is costly, while the adjoint system is typically ill-conditioned and indefinite. To address this issue, we propose an efficient implicit hypergradient method that approximates the lower-level response using finite, warm-started damped Gauss-Newton (GN) updates. For the adjoint solve, we use the damped GN matrix to compute an initial adjoint and to precondition a finite number of minimum residual iterations. To quantify the errors introduced by these approximations, we derive local hypergradient error bounds that separate the contributions of the finite lower-level solve, adjoint damping, and the final adjoint residual. Combining this analysis with validation sampling bounds and residual stability, we relate validation residuals to PDE solution accuracy and establish error bounds for the computed PDE solution. Numerical experiments on several nonlinear PDEs, including a high-dimensional problem, demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed method across Kansa, random feature and extreme learning machine, and physics-informed neural network solvers.

papers.title: When and why can integral constraints improve the accuracy of physics-informed neural networks?
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25515v1

summary.background:
- PDE (partial differential equation): an equation relating a function to its rates of change in several variables, used to model physical processes like heat or flow.
- PINN (physics-informed neural network): a neural network trained with a loss function that penalizes violations of the governing equation.
- Loss function: a score measuring how wrong the network is; training pushes it down.
- Integral constraint: an extra condition obtained by integrating (summing over space or time) the governing equation, added to the loss.
- Stability estimate: a mathematical bound showing that small errors in the loss cannot produce arbitrarily large errors in the solution.
- Error components: separate parts of the total error; the paper argues the standard loss controls some of these weakly.
summary.one_liner: The paper derives stability estimates for physics-informed neural network (PINN) losses with and without integral constraints for several PDEs, showing when integral constraints restore uniform control over certain error components, and checks this with numerical experiments.
summary.plain: Neural networks can be trained to approximate solutions of physics equations, such as heat or fluid flow equations, by penalizing them when they break those equations. Some researchers have found that also adding rules obtained by summing the equation over a region improves accuracy, but the reason was not well understood. This paper works out mathematically when that extra rule helps and shows that experiments agree with the explanation.
summary.why: It gives a theoretical reason for a practical training trick that has been reported to help in several applications, so users can predict when it is worth the effort. The text does not say how broadly the results extend beyond the PDEs studied, so that wider reach is uncertain.

papers.abstract: Adding constraints obtained by integrating governing equations to the loss has been reported to improve the accuracy of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) in several applications, but mathematical understanding of these benefits remains limited. For several partial differential equations (PDEs), we derive stability estimates for losses with and without integral constraints. The comparison reveals that in certain parameter regimes, the standard loss has very weak control over specific error components, and that the integral constraints restore uniform control of these components. This explains when and why the constraints improve accuracy. Finally, numerical experiments support this interpretation. In parameter regimes where the standard loss is predicted to have weak control over those components, the two losses indeed show clear differences in accuracy. Conversely, in regimes where the standard loss retains sufficient control, both losses yield similar accuracy.

papers.title: Variational integrators for time-dependent Lagrangian systems on Lie groups
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25313v1

summary.background:
- Lagrangian mechanics: motion is derived from an action (integral of kinetic minus potential energy) whose stationary paths give the equations of motion.
- Lie group: a smooth space with a compatible group multiplication, such as rotations SO(3); a Lie group is used to describe orientations.
- Variational integrator: a discrete-time scheme obtained by applying the action principle to a discretized action, which tends to inherit conservation laws.
- Symplectic map and Hamiltonian/momentum: geometric structure of phase space that conserved quantities (energy, momentum) respect.
- Noether's theorem: each continuous symmetry gives a conserved quantity.
- Backward error analysis: interprets a numerical scheme as the exact flow of a nearby "modified" system, explaining long-time accuracy.
- Consensus/synchronization: coupled agents reaching a common state; "local asymptotic stability" means nearby states converge back to that state.
summary.one_liner: The paper builds fixed-step variational integrators for time-dependent Lagrangian systems on Lie groups, analyzes their reduced dynamics, backward error, and long-time behavior, and proves stability and momentum-preservation results for an attitude consensus network on SO(3)^N.
summary.plain: The paper studies how to simulate on a computer the motion of rotating or orientation-like systems whose governing rules change over time, such as a spinning body or a group of coupled orientations. The authors design step-by-step numerical schemes built from a "discrete action" principle, which is meant to keep the simulation faithful to the underlying physics. They report that the schemes preserve key geometric structures, that the midpoint-Cayley version is second-order accurate, and that an extended energy quantity is nearly conserved over exponentially long times under stated assumptions.
summary.why: Structure-preserving integrators matter when simulations must run for long times without drifting away from physical laws, and the paper links this to attitude synchronization among coupled rotating bodies. The text does not show how widely these methods would be adopted, so their practical reach beyond the stated examples is uncertain.

papers.abstract: We develop fixed-step variational integrators for time-dependent Lagrangian systems on Lie groups, derive their reduced dynamics, and analyze their long-time behavior by backward error analysis. We derive the continuous Euler-Lagrange equations, energy balance, and Noether conservation laws, and construct time-indexed discrete Lagrangians using retractions, with the midpoint-Cayley scheme treated explicitly. On their regularity domains, the resulting phase-space maps are symplectic. For left-invariant discrete Lagrangians, they reduce to Lie-Poisson maps that preserve coadjoint orbits and, when $G$ is connected, every Casimir function. A variational error analysis establishes second-order accuracy of the midpoint-Cayley method. We also construct an exactly symplectic, projectable extension on $T^*(\mathbb R\times G)$ whose formal modified Hamiltonian is affine in the momentum conjugate to time and admits symmetry reduction. Under uniform analyticity, coefficient bounds, and domain-containment assumptions, optimal truncation yields exponentially accurate interpolation and near-conservation of the modified extended Hamiltonian over exponentially long intervals. For a connected attitude network on $SO(3)^N$ with damping and uniformly positive, non-increasing coupling weights, we prove local asymptotic stability of the static consensus set for the continuous dynamics and exact preservation of total spatial momentum by the discrete scheme. Numerical experiments on the network and on a time-dependent rigid body on $SO(3)$ illustrate second-order convergence and the extended energy balance.

papers.title: Stable admissible neural classes and convergent physics-informed neural networks
papers.label: arXiv:2611.24355v1

summary.background:
- PDE (partial differential equation): an equation relating a function to its rates of change in space, used to model physical systems such as heat or elasticity.
- Elliptic Dirichlet problem: a steady-state PDE with prescribed values on the boundary of the domain.
- Residual: how far a candidate solution is from satisfying the equation, evaluated at sample points.
- Least-squares loss: a training objective that sums squared residuals over points.
- Kansa collocation: a classical meshfree method that uses kernel functions and point-wise residuals, with an established convergence theory.
- Trial class: the family of functions (here neural networks) the approximate solution is searched within.
- Tanh-MLP: a multilayer perceptron, a standard feedforward neural network, using the tanh activation function.
- Stability and consistency: the two properties needed so that small discrete error implies small true error.
summary.one_liner: The paper extends the convergence theory of least-squares kernel collocation (Kansa) to neural trial classes for linear elliptic Dirichlet problems, establishing conditions under which tanh-MLP-based PINNs provably converge.
summary.plain: Neural-network methods such as PINNs solve equations describing physical systems by training a network to make the equation's residual small at sample points. This paper asks when that kind of training actually guarantees the network is close to the true solution, and it answers using tools from elliptic regularity (how smooth solutions of steady-state equations behave), discrete stability and consistency. It proves convergence for a constrained version using tanh networks, and gives a conditional result for the standard unconstrained PINN form under joint network and sampling refinement.
summary.why: Practitioners use PINNs widely but often without guarantees that a small training loss means a small solution error. The paper's framework may help clarify when such methods can be trusted, though the text alone does not show how well the conditions hold in practice.

papers.abstract: Residual-based methods, including physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), physics-informed Kolmogorov--Arnold networks, and some physics-informed neural operator architectures, approximate PDE solutions by minimizing a discrete least-squares loss formed from the PDE and boundary residuals over a prescribed trial class. This structure is shared by classical least-squares Kansa collocation, whose kernel trial spaces admit an established convergence theory. For neural trial classes, approximation power alone does not ensure that discrete residuals control the continuous solution error. For linear elliptic Dirichlet problems, we extend the kernel-based collocation framework to neural trial classes through elliptic regularity, discrete stability, and consistency. Elliptic regularity supplies the PDE estimate relating solution error to continuous residuals. Discrete stability identifies admissible trial subclasses in which continuous residuals are controlled by a computable discrete loss. This step also quantifies the required number of collocation points. Furthermore, the stability analysis naturally demands a scale-dependent, physics-balanced boundary weight. For the constrained problem, consistency requires accurate comparison functions within the same admissible subclass, a requirement not supplied by neural approximation estimates alone. Specializing to multilayer perceptrons with tanh activations (tanh-MLPs), we construct admissible comparison networks and establish convergence for the constrained residual minimization problem. We further obtain conditional convergence of unconstrained physics-balanced PINNs based on tanh-MLPs under joint network and sampling refinement.

papers.title: On global error estimates of a local discontinuous Galerkin method of the Boussinesq system of equations
papers.label: arXiv:2611.23901v1

summary.background:
- Boussinesq system: a set of partial differential equations coupling fluid velocity, pressure and temperature, used for buoyancy-driven flow.
- Finite element method: approximating a continuous problem by piecewise simple functions on a mesh.
- Discontinuous Galerkin (DG): a finite element variant that lets approximate functions jump between mesh cells, with "local" (LDG) referring to a specific way of handling derivatives.
- Upwind scheme: a stabilization that takes flow direction into account when computing transport terms.
- A priori error estimate: a bound on the approximation error derived before computing, in terms of mesh size and time step.
- Backward Euler: a simple implicit method for stepping forward in time.
- Uniform in time: the error bound stays controlled over arbitrarily long times, not just over a fixed interval.
summary.one_liner: The paper analyzes a local discontinuous Galerkin finite element scheme with upwind treatment of convective terms for the Boussinesq system, proving optimal a priori error estimates (including time-uniform bounds under smallness assumptions) for velocity, pressure and temperature, plus fully discrete backward Euler estimates.
summary.plain: The paper studies a numerical method for simulating the Boussinesq equations, a standard model of fluid flow where temperature differences drive motion, such as warm air rising in a room. The authors build a computational scheme that splits the domain into pieces and allows solutions to jump across their edges, then prove how close its approximate velocity, pressure and temperature stay to the true values. They also add a time-stepping version and report numerical experiments that the authors say support the theory.
summary.why: Mathematical guarantees on accuracy tell engineers and scientists how far to trust simulations of heat-driven flows, such as weather or industrial convection models. The text does not indicate how the results compare with existing methods beyond the stated analysis, so the practical reach is best judged by specialists.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we develop and analyze a local discontinuous Galerkin (LDG) finite element method for the Boussinesq system of equations, and employ an upwind scheme to effectively manage the nonlinear convective terms, thereby ensuring stability and accuracy. Our analysis establishes new \emph{a priori} regularity estimates for the semidiscrete LDG approximations. We establish optimal \emph{a priori} error estimates for the velocity approximation in $\bL^2$--norm, the pressure approximation in $L^2$--norm and for temperature in $L^2$--norm for all $t>0$. Our proof relies on the standard elliptic and parabolic duality arguments and modified Stokes operators defined on appropriate broken Sobolev spaces. Under suitable smallness assumptions on the given data, we further establish error estimates that remain uniform in time. Furthermore, the backward Euler scheme is considered for a full discretization, and optimal fully discrete error estimates are derived. Finally, we carry out numerical experiments to substantiate our theoretical findings.

papers.title: Finite element nonlinear nudging for the Navier-Stokes equations
papers.label: arXiv:2611.23036v1

summary.background:
- Navier-Stokes equations: the standard equations describing how viscous fluids such as air and water move.
- Data assimilation / nudging: adding a term to a simulation that pushes it toward real measurements, so the model tracks the actual system.
- Linear vs nonlinear nudging: linear nudging corrects in proportion to the error; the nonlinear version uses a stronger, nonlinear correction as the error gets smaller.
- Finite element method: a way of splitting a domain into small pieces (a mesh) to approximate solutions of differential equations, well suited to irregular shapes.
- Mesh size: the spacing of the grid; finer meshes give more accurate results but cost more computation.
- Implicit-explicit (IMEX) scheme: a time-stepping method that treats some terms implicitly for stability and others explicitly for speed.
- Inf-sup stability: a mathematical condition on the pairing of velocity and pressure approximations that prevents spurious numerical results.
- Super-exponential convergence: error shrinking faster than any simple exponential decay.
summary.one_liner: The paper analyzes an implicit-explicit finite element scheme for nonlinear nudging (data assimilation with a feedback term that grows stronger as the error shrinks) applied to the 3D incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, proving long-time stability and finite-time error convergence for the spatially semi-discrete scheme, with a mesh-resolution condition χ = O(H^{-1}) and numerical tests in 2D.
summary.plain: The paper studies how to pull a computer simulation of fluid flow (such as air or water moving around an object) onto the real flow, using sparse measurements taken from the actual flow. The authors use a correction term whose strength increases as the mismatch shrinks, which they report makes the simulation lock onto the true flow faster than the standard correction. The text reports that the method is proven stable and accurate under conditions on mesh size, and that tests on three 2D flows show faster synchronization, including when measurements cover only part of the region.
summary.why: Fluid flow prediction from partial, noisy observations matters for weather, ocean, and engineering modeling, and this work gives a finite element method (a standard tool for complex shapes and boundaries) with stated proofs for the nonlinear version. Its practical relevance beyond these test cases is not established by the text alone.

papers.abstract: Nonlinear nudging augments the classical linear nudging (continuous data as- similation) term with a nonlinear feedback that strengthens as the observed error decreases, and yields super-exponential convergence to the true state. In this paper, we study nonlinear nudging for the 3-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations with the finite element method, which allows complex geometries and physical boundary conditions. We propose an implicit-explicit (IMEX) finite element scheme with inf-sup stable elements, prove its unconditional long-time stability, and show for the spatially semi-discrete scheme that the error reaches a prescribed tolerance in finite time. Our analysis also suggests that the non- linear nudging term requires the mesh resolution to be fine enough (${χ= O(H^{-1})}$, where $χ$ is the nonlinear nudging intensity and ${H}$ is the observation mesh size). Further, our error estimates suggest that a larger nonlinear exponent $γ$ requires finer observational resolution, which is confirmed by numerical tests. Numerical experiments, including two-dimensional forced viscous flow in a periodic box, flow past a cylinder, and flow over a flat plate, show that nonlinear nudging synchronizes with the true solution considerably faster than linear nudging. We also show that observations in a subregion suffice to synchronize the whole flow

papers.title: Finite volume neural networks for singularly perturbed boundary value problems
papers.label: arXiv:2611.22066v1

summary.background:
- Boundary value problem: an equation solved on a region with values fixed at its edges.
- Singular perturbation: a small parameter multiplies the highest-order derivative, so the solution changes abruptly in a thin boundary layer.
- Boundary-layer corrector: an added term that captures the rapid change near the edge.
- Finite volume method: a numerical method that enforces conservation by balancing fluxes across the faces of small cells.
- Physics-informed neural network (PINN): a neural network trained to satisfy the governing equation and boundary conditions.
- Convection-dominated / Burgers-type problems: transport-heavy equations where shocks or steep fronts can form.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes sl-FVNN, a finite volume neural network augmented with analytically derived boundary-layer correctors, to solve singularly perturbed boundary value problems and compares it with singular-layer PINNs on reaction-diffusion and Burgers-type equations.
summary.plain: The paper looks at equations where a tiny parameter makes the solution change very sharply in a thin strip near the edge of the domain. The authors build a neural-network solver that enforces conservation of quantities over small cells, and adds known mathematical correction terms for those thin edge regions. Their tests cover very small parameter values, from 10^-4 down to 10^-12, and they report more uniform accuracy and better convergence than a conventional version of the method.
summary.why: Sharp, thin-layer behavior is hard for standard solvers, including neural ones, so a method that handles it stably is of practical interest for multiscale modeling. The text claims comparable accuracy to an existing physics-informed approach on some problems and better convergence on convection-dominated nonlinear ones; the evidence is limited to the abstract, so these claims are not independently checked here.

papers.abstract: We develop a singular-layer enhanced Finite Volume Neural Network (sl-FVNN) methodology for solving singularly perturbed boundary value problems. The proposed framework combines flux-conserving finite volume residuals with analytically derived boundary layer correctors, enabling stable and efficient approximation of sharp boundary variations induced by small perturbation parameters. Numerical experiments over a broad range of small perturbation parameters ($10^{-4}$ to $10^{-12}$), demonstrate that the sl-FVNN yields uniformly accurate predicted solutions and significantly improved convergence behavior compared to conventional FVNN methods. Further comparisons with sl-PINNs from (Gie, Hong, Jung, Appl. Anal. 2024) show that our sl-FVNNs attain comparable accuracy for reaction--diffusion and Burgers equations, while achieving significantly improved convergence for convection-dominated nonlinear problems. These results highlight the effectiveness of incorporating asymptotic layer structures into finite volume based neural networks, offering a practical and scalable framework for multiscale PDE learning in stiff regimes.

papers.title: Direct Element-Level Mass Matrix Inversion
papers.label: arXiv:2611.21820v1

summary.background:
- Finite element method: splitting a solid object into small connected pieces (elements) and solving equations for each piece.
- Mass matrix: a table describing how the element's mass is spread across its corner points (nodes); it sets how the element resists acceleration.
- Lumped mass: a simplified version that puts all mass on the nodes, giving a diagonal table that is trivial to invert.
- Consistent mass: a fuller version that spreads mass between nodes, which needs a system of equations to solve.
- Explicit time integration: a stepping scheme that advances the simulation without solving a large global system at each step, valued for speed.
- Isoparametric and higher-order elements: elements with curved edges or extra mid-side nodes, giving more accurate shapes and fields.
- Element-by-element: a computing approach that works on one element at a time rather than assembling a global matrix.
summary.one_liner: The paper derives a systematic, closed-form way to invert element-level mixed (lumped plus consistent) mass matrices for isoparametric solid elements of arbitrary order, with an explicit inverse given for the eight-node hexahedral element, for use in explicit transient dynamics.
summary.plain: Engineers simulating fast-moving solids, such as impacts or crashes, often use a simplified way of representing mass that makes each time step cheap to compute. This paper looks at when that simplification is too crude, especially for more detailed element shapes and poor-quality meshes. It presents a method for computing the exact inverse of a blended mass description directly at the level of each element, and works this out explicitly for a common eight-corner brick-shaped element.
summary.why: The text suggests that better inertia modelling could widen the use of higher-order elements in explicit simulations while keeping their speed. The text does not report test results or timings, so how much accuracy or speed is gained is not shown here.

papers.abstract: Explicit finite element methods for transient solid dynamics commonly use lumped mass matrices to avoid solving systems of equations for nodal accelerations at each time step. However, diagonal mass matrices may inadequately represent inertia, particularly for higher-order elements and coarse or distorted meshes. This has limited the use of higher-order elements in explicit dynamic analyses. This paper presents a systematic method for directly evaluating the inverse of non-diagonal element-level mass matrices for solid isoparametric elements of arbitrary interpolation order. The method applies to mixed mass matrices defined as linear combinations of lumped and consistent mass matrices, with a weighting parameter controlling the transition between diagonal, consistent, and intermediate formulations. It therefore provides a framework for incorporating non-diagonal mass formulations, including those for quadratic elements, into explicit finite element algorithms. The approach is demonstrated by deriving an explicit inverse formula for the mixed mass matrix of the eight-node hexahedral element. This formula enables efficient element-level inversion without solving a global system. The proposed method can improve inertial representation in transient dynamic analyses while retaining the computational advantages of explicit time integration and is suitable for element-by-element implementations.

papers.title: Maximum principle preserving approximation of scalar conservation equations with a fractional Laplacian
papers.label: arXiv:2611.20833v1

summary.background:
- Scalar conservation law: an equation saying a quantity is moved around by a flow without being created or destroyed.
- Fractional Laplacian (order s between 0 and 1): a long-range diffusion operator, a spreading process where distant points interact, unlike ordinary local diffusion.
- Finite element method: approximating a solution by simple pieces over a mesh of the domain.
- Maximum principle: the numerical solution stays between its smallest and largest starting values.
- Sinc quadrature: a numerical technique for approximating an integral-based operator by a sum of simpler terms.
- Graph viscosity and convex limiting: artificial damping added to suppress spurious oscillations while keeping accuracy where the solution is smooth.
- Strong stability preserving Runge–Kutta: a class of time-stepping schemes designed not to create new extremes.
- CFL condition: a limit on time-step size relative to mesh size needed for stability.
summary.one_liner: A continuous finite element method for scalar conservation laws with a fractional diffusion term of order s in (0,1), using sinc-quadrature resolvents, graph viscosity, and convex limiting to preserve the maximum principle and reach second-order accuracy.
summary.plain: The paper concerns computer simulation of equations describing how a quantity such as concentration or temperature is carried by a flow and also spreads out in a long-range way, rather than only locally. The authors build a numerical method that keeps the computed values within their physically allowed range (for example, staying nonnegative) and conserves the total amount. They report a first-order version that provably has this property under a time-step limit, and a higher-order version that keeps the property while being second-order accurate in tests.
summary.why: Keeping simulated values physically plausible while using higher-order accuracy is a standard concern in numerical modelling of transport. The text says the method is tested on the Surface Quasi-Geostrophic equation, a model used in geophysical fluid dynamics, and on unstructured meshes; wider impact beyond these tests is not shown in the text.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose a maximum principle preserving continuous finite element method for scalar conservation laws augmented with a fractional diffusion operator of order $s\in (0,1)$. Conservation laws with fractional diffusion operators arise in a variety of physical models involving anomalous transport and nonlocal regularization, including geophysical flows, plasma physics, and nonlinear acoustics. The fractional Laplacian is approximated using a sinc-quadrature representation, yielding a resolvent-based formulation compatible with continuous finite elements and explicit strong stability preserving Runge--Kutta time integration. A first-order monotone scheme is constructed using graph viscosity and is shown to satisfy a discrete maximum principle under an explicit CFL condition. A high-order extension is obtained via entropy-consistent corrections and convex limiting, achieving second-order accuracy while preserving the maximum principle, and hence positivity, as well as mass conservation in the periodic setting. Numerical experiments, including applications to the Surface Quasi-Geostrophic equation, confirm the second-order accuracy and the robustness of the proposed method on unstructured meshes.
